Vlad sits down with Robert O’Neill and Nicholas Irving for a candid, unfiltered discussion about deployment culture in Afghanistan and the Middle East. O’Neill recalls a shocking exchange with an Afghan interpreter he nicknamed “Larry,” who claimed sex with animals was acceptable only with females, sparking a broader conversation about power, sexuality, Pakistan’s influence, Karachi, Dubai supply routes, the Taliban, and wartime rumors around Osama bin Laden’s compound in Pakistan.

The conversation later shifts to veterans’ issues after Vlad mentions Craigslist founder Craig Newmark’s plan to donate $1 billion, largely toward military veterans. O’Neill and Irving discuss VA bureaucracy, PTSD claims, combat disability, transition challenges after service, and the growing conversation around psychedelics as a possible tool for veteran mental health support. A raw look at war stories, dark humor, and the serious realities facing U.S. veterans.

Denvonta “Dirt Rocc” Lee sits down with Vlad to recount taking the stand against Keefe D after roughly 15 years without seeing him in person. Lee describes the tension inside the courtroom, their past dispute over money, and what he says was Keefe D’s angry reaction in front of the jury. The conversation also addresses Lee’s claim that he heard talk of a “green light” allegedly being placed on him, while Vlad questions how much impact his testimony actually had on the murder trial.

The interview covers Reggie Wright Jr.’s testimony, Judge Mathis’ legal analysis, Nevada’s unanimous jury rules, and the surprise of a verdict returning in about 90 minutes. Lee explains why he avoided watching the trial, why he believed there was still a chance for a hung jury, and how he reacted when news of Keefe D’s conviction reached him.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Rex Holloway recalls entering Texas state prison at 17 and facing adult inmates, solitary confinement, and the harsh intake process at Huntsville’s Holiday Unit. Holloway describes the 1980s Texas prison system as violent and tightly controlled, with “building tenders” acting as inmate guards before the Ruiz lawsuit helped end the practice. He discusses claims that guards and inmate enforcers could kill prisoners and hide the evidence, pointing viewers to the Texas Prison Museum for context. Holloway also breaks down the rise of prison groups after the power vacuum, including the Texas Syndicate, Texas Aryan Brotherhood, Aryan Brotherhood of Texas, Aryan Circle, and White Knights, while explaining how ABT differed from the California Aryan Brotherhood. The conversation also touches on racial politics, extortion, prison myths, and comments from former Mexican Mafia hitman Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza explains how the Mexican Mafia’s influence moved between prison and the streets, from LA County Jail and level four prisons to Folsom and San Quentin. Mendoza breaks down why the term “contract hit” often didn’t mean payment, but an obligation tied to Mafia politics, loyalty, and survival. He discusses how members once handled violence themselves before the 1990s shift toward using street gang members, Sureños, money earners, and enforcers.

Mendoza also reflects on Peg Leg Joe, insulation from violence, heroin and cocaine connections, and the changing underworld structure. Later, he recalls Alfie’s arrest in Tijuana by Baja California State Police, extradition to the U.S., and a Fresno preliminary hearing involving the Gilbert Roybal homicide, where a bizarre Mickey Rooney confession twist surfaced in court.

--------
In this VladTV conversation, Royce White and DJ Vlad debate abortion, faith, poverty, and the value of human life from sharply different perspectives. Vlad, a father with planned children, argues for understanding the realities of unplanned pregnancy, while White cites Planned Parenthood statistics, his Catholic beliefs, and his own upbringing by a working-class Black single mother to defend a pro-life position.

The discussion expands into broader cultural issues, including Christianity, birth control, the Catholic Church, economic struggle, and whether society’s view of life connects to violence in places like Chicago. White also references Trick Daddy’s family background, the Lindsay Clancy case, King Von, Bloodhound Q50, the Ukraine war, and the military-industrial complex while making his case about desensitization and modern culture.

Despite clear disagreements, Vlad and Royce keep the conversation civil, contrasting it with more heated podcast debates and showing how divisive topics can still be discussed respectfully.
